Within capacity by 1,000 lb using the 30-ft row.

rationales: This forgets the deductions. Everything below the boom tip that the chart says to deduct counts against capacity, so the total is 8,000 lb.
This adds the rigging but leaves out the hook block. The chart says to deduct the block as well, so the total is 8,000 lb.
3.5 tons × 2,000 lb = 7,000 lb. Add the 600 lb block and 400 lb of rigging: 7,000 + 600 + 400 = 8,000 lb.
This uses 2,200 lb per ton. A US ton is 2,000 lb, so the machine weighs 7,000 lb and the total is 8,000 lb.
beyond: Read the chart notes for each job. On some charts the block weight is already deducted and on others it is not, and deducting it twice or not at all both give the wrong margin.
fact: Converting tons to pounds and adding every chart deduction to get the weight the chart must cover.

stem: A pump skid's weight is unknown. It will be picked at 40 ft radius and set at 60 ft. The chart rates 32,000 lb at 40 ft and 24,000 lb at 60 ft. The operator will check the weight with the load moment indicator at lift-off. Above what reading must the operator stop and verify the weight another way?
rationales: The longest radius used is 60 ft, rated at 24,000 lb. 75% of 24,000 = 24,000 − 6,000 = 18,000 lb.
This is 75% of the 32,000 lb rating at 40 ft, which is the pick radius. It also equals the full 60 ft rating. The rule uses 75% at the longest radius, which is 18,000 lb.
This is 80% of 24,000. The percentage is wrong. The rule uses 75%, which gives 18,000 lb.
This takes 75% of the average of the two ratings (28,000 lb). The rule uses the capacity at the longest radius, not an average.

quotes.quote: if it exceeds 75 percent of the maximum rated capacity at the longest radius that will be used during the lift operation

beyond: Quick method: 75% is the number minus a quarter of itself. A quarter of 24,000 is 6,000, so 75% is 18,000.
fact: Working out the 75% verification threshold from the capacity at the longest radius of the lift.

stem: An outrigger float measures 2 ft by 2 ft. It will carry 40,000 lb and sits centered on a 4 ft by 4 ft timber mat. Treat the mat as rigid and ignore its weight. What is the average pressure on the ground under the mat?
choices: 10,000 psf: 40,000 lb on the 4 sq ft float
2,500 psf: 40,000 lb spread over the 16 sq ft mat
625 psf: 10,000 lb per outrigger over 16 sq ft
5,000 psf: 40,000 lb over 8 sq ft (4 + 4)
rationales: This is the pressure under the float, on top of the mat. The ground sees the load spread over the mat's 16 sq ft, so 2,500 psf.
Mat area = 4 ft × 4 ft = 16 sq ft. Pressure = 40,000 ÷ 16 = 2,500 lb per sq ft.
This splits the 40,000 lb among four outriggers again, but the 40,000 lb is already the load on this one outrigger. The answer is 40,000 ÷ 16 = 2,500 psf.
This adds the sides instead of multiplying them. Area is length × width, 4 × 4 = 16 sq ft, so the pressure is 2,500 psf.
misconceptions: used float area instead of mat area
dividing outrigger load by four again
beyond: Doubling both mat dimensions makes the area four times larger and cuts the pressure to one quarter. That is why a modest increase in mat size helps so much.
fact: Ground bearing pressure is the load divided by the area of the mat in square feet.

stem: A precast concrete block measures 4 ft by 3 ft by 2 ft. Using 150 lb per cubic foot for concrete, what does the block weigh?
rationales: Volume = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cu ft. Weight = 24 × 150 = 3,600 lb.
This uses only two dimensions (4 × 3 = 12 sq ft), which is a face area, not a volume. Multiplying by the 2 ft height as well gives 24 cu ft and 3,600 lb.
This rounds the block up to a full cubic yard (27 cu ft). The block is actually 24 cu ft, so it weighs 3,600 lb.
This adds the dimensions (4 + 3 + 2 = 9) instead of multiplying them. Volume is 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cu ft, so the block weighs 3,600 lb.
misconceptions: cubic yard substituted for actual volume
beyond: Embedded steel, lifting inserts and attached hardware add weight. Treat a volume estimate as a minimum and verify it if the block is near the chart limit.
fact: Calculating a load's weight from volume (length × width × height) and density.

stem: Chart for 80 ft of main boom: 30 ft radius, 20,000 lb; 35 ft radius, 16,000 lb; 40 ft radius, 13,000 lb. Chart notes: use the next longer radius when between listed radii; deduct the hook block (800 lb) and the stowed jib (1,200 lb). The lift will be made at 33 ft. What is the largest load, including its slings, the crane can lift?
choices: 18,000 lb: 20,000 at 30 ft minus 2,000 deductions
16,000 lb: 35 ft chart value, deductions ignored
14,000 lb: 16,000 at 35 ft minus the 2,000 deductions
15,600 lb: 17,600 at 33 ft minus 2,000 deductions
rationales: This uses the shorter radius, whose capacity is higher than the crane's capacity at 33 ft. The chart note requires the next longer radius, 35 ft.
The radius is right, but the block and stowed jib must come off the chart value. That leaves 14,000 lb.
33 ft falls between listed radii, so use 35 ft: 16,000 lb. Deductions are 800 + 1,200 = 2,000 lb, so 16,000 − 2,000 = 14,000 lb.
This interpolates 3/5 of the way from 20,000 to 16,000. The chart says to use the next longer radius, not to interpolate.
beyond: Measure radius with the load suspended. Boom deflection pushes the radius out, and if the 33 ft lift drifts past 35 ft, the next column (13,000 lb) governs.
fact: Combining the next-longer-radius rule with chart deductions to find the largest allowable load.

stem: A crawler crane will pick a vessel of unknown weight at 30 ft radius and set it at 50 ft. The chart rates 40,000 lb at 30 ft and 20,000 lb at 50 ft. At lift-off the load moment indicator shows 16,000 lb. What must the operator do?
choices: Stop and verify the weight: 16,000 exceeds 75% of 20,000 lb
Stop and reduce the load: 16,000 exceeds the 75% limit at 50 ft
Proceed: 16,000 is below the full 20,000 lb rating at 50 ft
Proceed: 16,000 is below 75% of the 40,000 lb rating at 30 ft
rationales: The longest radius is 50 ft, and 75% of 20,000 = 15,000 lb. The 16,000 lb reading is above that, so the lift cannot proceed until the weight is verified by a recognized source or calculation.
75% only triggers verification. It is not a capacity limit. Once verified, a load up to the full rating can be lifted, so reducing the load is not what the rule requires.
The load may well be within capacity, but an indicator reading above 75% at the longest radius requires verification before proceeding.
75% of 40,000 is 30,000, but 30 ft is the pick radius. The rule measures at the longest radius used, which is 50 ft.

quotes.quote: If it does, the operator must not proceed with the lift until he/she verifies the weight of the load in accordance with paragraph (o)(3)(i) of this section.

beyond: Indicators read gross load and can be thrown off by dynamics or wrong configuration settings. Verifying the weight protects against an indicator that reads low.
fact: Applying the 75% verification rule when pick and set radii differ, and what the operator must do when the load exceeds it.

stem: A 5-ton (US) load is rigged with a 1,500 lb hook block and 500 lb of rigging. The chart capacity at the working radius is 15,000 lb, and the block and rigging both count against it. What percent of capacity is the lift?
choices: 77%: 11,500 lb, no rigging
80%: 12,000 lb in total
67%: 10,000 lb, load only
rationales: This adds the block but forgets the 500 lb of rigging. The gross load is 12,000 lb, or 80%.
This uses 2,200 lb per ton, which gives 11,000 + 2,000. A US ton is 2,000 lb, so the total is 12,000 lb, or 80%.
This leaves out the block and rigging. Both count against capacity, so the gross load is 12,000 lb, or 80%.
beyond: For percentages without a calculator, simplify the fraction first: 12,000/15,000 = 12/15 = 4/5 = 80%.
fact: Finding the lift's percentage of capacity after converting tons and adding the block and rigging.

stem: Chart capacity at the working radius is 8,000 lb, and the chart note says to deduct the 500 lb hook block. The spreader bar and slings weigh 1,100 lb. Each pipe is 20 ft long at 30 lb per foot. What is the most pipes that can go in one lift?
choices: 13 pipes: full 8,000 lb ÷ 600 lb
11 pipes: 10.7 rounded to nearest
12 pipes: 7,500 lb ÷ 600 lb
10 pipes: 6,400 lb ÷ 600 lb each
rationales: This uses the chart value with no deductions. Taking off the block and rigging leaves 6,400 lb, which allows 10 pipes.
Rounding a piece count to the nearest whole number can push the load over capacity. 11 pipes weigh 6,600 lb, more than the 6,400 lb available, so round down.
This deducts the hook block but forgets the 1,100 lb spreader and slings. Only 6,400 lb is available.
8,000 − 500 − 1,100 = 6,400 lb available. Each pipe is 20 × 30 = 600 lb. 6,400 ÷ 600 = 10.7, which rounds down to 10 (6,000 lb). 11 pipes would weigh 6,600 lb.
beyond: Round in the direction that protects the crane. Round load weights up, and round capacities and piece counts down.
fact: Dividing the available capacity by the weight per piece and rounding down to a whole number of pieces.
